From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

Created by President Harry S. Truman in 1945 as the Medal of Freedom, the medal was renamed by President John F. Kennedy in 1963 as the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Executive Order 11085 (February 22, 1963) allows the President to recognize "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."

The medal is a white star over a red pentagon, surrounded by five gold eagles. At the star's center is a blue circle with 13 gold stars. The Presidential Medal of Freedom comes in two degrees, with the more prestigious version known as the Presidential Medal of Freedom "with distinction."

There is no formal procedure for nominating and selecting recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The President has wide latitude under Executive Order 11515 (March 13, 1970) to award the medal to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative." Selections often reflect the President's political and personal interests.

Numerous Members of Congress have sent nominations to the President. Some Members have made floor remarks about potential or past recipients and introduced resolutions congratulating honorees or urging the President to recognize a specific individual.

Between 1963 and 2026, the Presidential Medal of Freedom was awarded 675 times to 672 individuals and one group (the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team); two people (Ellsworth Bunker and Colin Powell) received the medal twice. This report contains a comprehensive list of honorees and indicates the 56 medals known to have been awarded "with distinction."

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is considered the U.S. government's highest civilian honor. Awarded by the President, it is often presented to individuals to recognize a lifetime of significant achievements in the arts, public service, science, or other fields.

This report describes the history of the medal, provides information about its design and related protocol, and discusses the nomination and selection process. It concludes with tables containing a comprehensive list of honorees since 1963.

In July 1945, President Harry S. Truman issued an executive order, near the end of World War II, to create the Medal of Freedom. In establishing the award, he sought to honor civilians who "performed a meritorious act or service which has aided the United States" or one of its allies overseas during wartime, "and for which an award of another United States medal or decoration is considered inappropriate."[1](#fn1 "Executive Order 9586, ") During the Korean War, President Truman expanded the medal's eligibility to include actions during "any period of national emergency."[2](#fn2 "Executive Order 10336, ") It was awarded thousands of times, mostly by federal officials other than the President.[3](#fn3 "Bruce Wetterau, The Presidential Medal of Freedom: Winners and Their Achievements (Washington: Congressional Quarterly Inc., 1996), p. 9.")

In his 1955 State of the Union address, President Dwight D. Eisenhower called for "awards of merit … whereby we can honor our fellow citizens who make great contribution to the advancement of our civilization."[4](#fn4) The House twice passed bills to create a Medal for Distinguished Civilian Achievement: H.R. 11923 in the 84th Congress[5](#fn5 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 2, 1956), p. 11609.") and H.R. 488 in the 85th Congress.[6](#fn6 "Congressional Record , vol. 104, part 11 (July 23, 1958), p. 14794.") In each case, the Senate referred the bill to committee and took no further action.[7](#fn7 "Congressional Record , vol. 102, part 9 (July 3, 1956), p. 11678 and vol. 104, part 11 (July 24, 1958), p. 14895.")

In 1963, President John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11085 to modify the Medal of Freedom, including by giving it a new name: the Presidential Medal of Freedom. It would now be awarded solely by the President to "any person who has made an especially meritorious contribution to (1) the security or national interests of the United States, or (2) world peace, or (3) cultural or other significant public or private endeavors."[8](#fn8 "Executive Order 11085, ")

President Kennedy said at the time that

in a period when the national government must call upon an increasing portion of the talents and energies of its citizens, it is clearly appropriate to provide ways to recognize and reward the work of persons, within and without the government, who contribute significantly to the quality of American life.[9](#fn9)

On July 4, 1963, President Kennedy announced the first slate of 31 honorees.[10](#fn10 "Ibid., p. 210 (in note) .") President Lyndon B. Johnson presented the initial Presidential Medals of Freedom two weeks after President Kennedy's assassination, with two posthumous additions to the list: Pope John XXIII and President Kennedy.[11](#fn11)

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is a white star over a red pentagon, surrounded by five gold eagles. At the star's center is a blue circle with 13 gold stars.

Harry D. Temple, the head of the Army's Institute of Heraldry, designed the medal with input from President Kennedy and First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy.[12](#fn12 "Jenifer V. Buckman, ") A contemporary White House document described the white star—a symbol displayed on military vehicles—as "the identifying emblem of United States elements in the defense of freedom" and "recognized universally as a symbol of our selfless determination to maintain the freedom and democracy of mankind."[13](#fn13)

The Presidential Medal of Freedom comes in two degrees, with the more prestigious version known as the Presidential Medal of Freedom "with distinction."

At the first White House awards ceremony, President Johnson described the Presidential Medal of Freedom as "the Nation's highest civil honor."[14](#fn14) It has also been described as "the civilian equivalent of the Congressional Medal of Honor"[15](#fn15) and "the highest civil award that can be presented by the President of the United States."[16](#fn16 "Lawrence M. Watson, The Presidential Medal of Freedom (Claymont, DE: Orders and Medals Society of America, 2014) , p. 39.")

Guides to etiquette and precedence typically list the Presidential Medal of Freedom first among nonmilitary U.S. awards.[17](#fn17 "Mary Mel French, United States Protocol: The Guide to Official Diplomatic Etiquette (Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, 2010), p p. 271 , 275 ; Department of the Army, Guide to the Wear and Appearance of Army Uniforms and Insignia , Pamphlet 670-1, January 26, 2021, p. 260, at https://armypubs.army.mil/epubs/DR_pubs/DR_a/ARN30948-PAM_670-1-000-WEB-1.pdf#page=277 ; and Article 5307 in Navy Personnel Command, United States Navy Uniform Regulations , NAVPERS 15665J, at...")

Nomination, Selection, and Presentation

There is no formal procedure for nominations or the evaluation of potential recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom.[18](#fn18 "Juliet Eilperin, ")

The President can award the medal to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative."[19](#fn19 "Executive Order 11515, ") Selections often reflect the President's political and personal interests.

The medal is often, though not always, presented at an annual White House ceremony.[20](#fn20 "For example, see videos available online from the 1981 ceremony (at https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/video/medal-freedom-ceremony-president-reagan-gives-remarks-and-presents-awards-east-room ) and the 2022 ceremony (at https://www.c-span.org/video/?521521-1/presidential-medal-freedom-ceremony ).")

Role for Members of Congress

Numerous Members have sent nominations to the President, often in a formal written letter.[21](#fn21 "For example, see Rep. Lee H. Hamilton, ")

Some Members have also made floor remarks and inserted statements into the *Congressional Record* about potential or past recipients.[22](#fn22 "For example, see Sen. Max Cleland, ")

In addition, some Members have introduced resolutions urging the President to recognize specific people with the award,[23](#fn23 "For example, see S.Res. 23 (107 th Cong.) for Benjamin Elijah Mays, H.Con.Res. 313 (108 th Cong.) for Pope John Paul II, S.Con.Res. 91 (109 th Cong.) for Satchel Paige, H.Res. 926 (114 th Cong.) for Henrietta Lacks, and S.Con.Res. 20 (116 th Cong.) for Harry W. Colmery.") and to congratulate or memorialize honorees.[24](#fn24 "For example, see S.Res. 310 (107 th Cong.) for Justin Dart Jr. , H.Res. 708 (111 th Cong.) for Nancy Brinker , H.Res. 1743 (111 th Cong.) for Gerda Weissmann Klein , and S.Res. 61 (117 th Cong.) for George P. Shultz.")

In recent years, some Members have also asked the President to revoke a previously awarded medal.[25](#fn25 "H.R. 4354 (114 th Cong. ) and H.R. 6810 (115 th Cong. ) expressed the sense of Congress that Bill Cosby's medal, awarded in 2002, should be revoked.") President Barack H. Obama said in 2015 there was "no precedent for revoking the medal."[26](#fn26 "Krishnadev Calamur, ")

Recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom

The Presidential Medal of Freedom was awarded 675 times between 1963 and 2026.[27](#fn27 "To compile this list, CRS searched Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States volumes for 1963 to 2016, and the Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents for 2017 to the present , for mentions of the medal. Additional recipients were identified using the Weekly Compilation of Presidential Documents , contemporaneous news reports , and White House press releases . In comp iling this list, CRS attempted to be thorough ; however , the list of medals in this rep...")

The recipients included 672 individuals and one group, the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team.[28](#fn28 "While awarding the medal to the Apollo 13 Mission Operations Team, President Richard M. Nixon mentioned five individuals: Sig Sjoberg, Glynn Lunney, Milt Windler, Gerald Griffin, and Gene Krantz. See ") Two people received the medal twice: Ellsworth Bunker (in 1963 and 1967) and Colin Powell (in 1991 and 1993).

An academic analysis of recipients through 2013 found the most common primary area of achievement was political and public service (about 27% of recipients), followed by art, acting, and music (about 15%) and academia and science (about 14%). Additional areas of achievement included civil rights (about 9% of recipients), humanitarianism and philanthropy (about 6%), military service (about 6%), and journalism and broadcasting (about 6%). Smaller numbers of recipients were recognized for achievements in writing and literature, athletics, labor, business, religion, conservation and environmentalism, and architecture and engineering.[29](#fn29 "Kyle C. Kopko et al . , ")

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg/250px-Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg)

The [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom")

This is a partial **list of recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom**, listed chronologically within the aspect of life in which each recipient is or was renowned.

The [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") is awarded by the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative".[[1]](#cite_note-1) Before 1970, honorees were either selected by the president or recommended to them by the [Distinguished Civilian Service Awards Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Civilian_Service_Awards_Board "Distinguished Civilian Service Awards Board").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_recipients&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Typically the medal is bestowed upon the recipient by the sitting president who has chosen them. However, the first recipients selected by president [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") before [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") were formally awarded by his successor in office, [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson").[[3]](#cite_note-id26165-3)

President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") awarded 118 medals, the most of any president, followed by President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") with 89 medal recipients.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Three people—[Ellsworth Bunker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellsworth_Bunker "Ellsworth Bunker"), [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell"), and [Ben Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Carson "Ben Carson")—are two-time recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Powell received his second award with distinction, while Bunker was given both of his awards with distinction.[[5]](#cite_note-2ndPMoF-5)

Eight presidents have themselves received the medal posthumously, post-presidency, or prior to being elected:

* [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") (1963, posthumously)
* [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson") (1980, posthumously)
* [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") (1993, with distinction)
* [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford") (1999)
* [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") (1999)
* [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") (2011)
* [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") (2013)
* [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (2017, as Vice President; with distinction)

In 2015, Obama stated that there was no precedent to revoke a Presidential Medal of Freedom, regarding the award given to stand-up comedian and actor [Bill Cosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby "Bill Cosby").[[6]](#cite_note-6) After being awarded the medal in 2002 by Obama's predecessor, [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), Cosby was [convicted of multiple counts of sexual assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby_sexual_assault_cases "Bill Cosby sexual assault cases"), though the convictions were later overturned.[[7]](#cite_note-ctv-overturned-7)

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is related to, but distinct from, the [Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Freedom_(1945) "Medal of Freedom (1945)"), an earlier award issued between 1945 and 1963 to honor US civilian contributions to [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

In 2022 at the age of 25, athlete and activist [Simone Biles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_Biles "Simone Biles") became the youngest person to receive the award.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

### Declinations of the award

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_recipients&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Declinations of the award")]

[Bill Belichick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Belichick "Bill Belichick"), coach of the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots"), was offered the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), and initially accepted it, but changed his mind and turned down the medal after the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Country musician [Dolly Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Parton "Dolly Parton") turned down the medal twice from Donald Trump. Parton said she turned it down the first time because her husband was ill, and the second time because of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[10]](#cite_note-10)

American cultural anthropologist (1901–1978)

"Margaret Bateson" redirects here. For the British journalist and activist, see [Margaret Heitland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Heitland "Margaret Heitland").

Not to be confused with the British anthropologist [Margaret Read](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Read_(anthropologist) "Margaret Read (anthropologist)").

**Ariel Durant** ([/dəˈrænt/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born **Chaya Kaufman**; May 10, 1898 – October 25, 1981)[[1]](#cite_note-NYT-1) was a Ukrainian-born American researcher and writer. She was the coauthor of *[The Story of Civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_of_Civilization "The Story of Civilization")* with her husband, [Will Durant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Durant "Will Durant"). They were awarded the [Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_General_Nonfiction "Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction").

## Biography

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ariel_Durant&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Ariel_and_Will_Durant.jpg/250px-Ariel_and_Will_Durant.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ariel_and_Will_Durant.jpg)

Ariel and Will Durant in the library of their home in Los Angeles, 1967

Durant was born Chaya Kaufman in [Proskurov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proskurov "Proskurov"), [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") (now [Khmelnytskyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmelnytskyi "Khmelnytskyi"), Ukraine), to [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Russia "History of the Jews in Russia") parents Ethel Appel Kaufman and Joseph Kaufman. Ariel later went by Ida.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) The family emigrated in 1900, living for several months in London 1900–01 en route to the United States, where they arrived in 1901. She had three older sisters, Sarah, Mary, and Flora, and three older brothers, Harry, Maurice, and Michael.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) Flora became Ariel's companion and sometime assistant, and moved with the Durants to California.

She met her future husband when she was a student at Ferrer [Modern School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_School_(United_States) "Modern School (United States)") in New York City. He was then a teacher at the school, but resigned his post to marry Ariel. At the time of the wedding, on October 31, 1913, Ariel was 15 and Will Durant was nearly 28 years old.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The wedding took place at [New York City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Hall "New York City Hall"), to which she roller-skated from her family's home in [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"). The couple had one daughter, Ethel Benvenuta Durant (1919–1986)[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) and adopted a son, Louis Richard "Lipschultz" Durant (1917–2008) who was the son of Ariel's sister Flora Kaufman Lipschultz and her former husband, Joseph Bernard Lipschultz (divorced 1928).[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Louis had lived in Will and Ariel's home with his mother, Flora, when he was quite young (1920 Census).

Ariel Durant legally changed her first name to Ariel after [the character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_(The_Tempest) "Ariel (The Tempest)") from Shakespeare's *[The Tempest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tempest "The Tempest")*, which was the nickname her husband gave her because he said she was "strong and brave as a boy, and as swift and mischievous as an elf".[[1]](#cite_note-NYT-1)

The Durants were awarded the [Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_General_Nonfiction "Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction") in 1968 for *[Rousseau and Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rousseau_and_Revolution "Rousseau and Revolution")*, the tenth volume of *The Story of Civilization*. In 1977 they were presented with the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") by [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford"), and Ariel was named "Woman of the Year" by the city of Los Angeles. The Durants received the Golden Plate Award of the [American Academy of Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Achievement "Academy of Achievement") in 1976.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The Durants wrote a 420-page joint autobiography, published by Simon & Schuster in 1978 (*A Dual Autobiography*; later [ISBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISBN_(identifier) "ISBN (identifier)") [0-671-23078-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:BookSources/0-671-23078-6 "Special:BookSources/0-671-23078-6")).

The Durants died within two weeks of each other in 1981, with Ariel dying on October 25 and Will following on November 7.[[5]](#cite_note-5) and are buried at the [Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westwood_Village_Memorial_Park_Cemetery "Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery") in Los Angeles, California. Ariel told Ethel's daughter, Monica Mehill, that it was their differences that made them grow.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)

**Helen Adams Keller** (June 27, 1880 – June 1, 1968) was an American [deafblind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deafblind "Deafblind") author, [disability rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_rights "Disability rights") advocate, political activist and lecturer.

Born in West [Tuscumbia, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuscumbia,_Alabama "Tuscumbia, Alabama"), she [lost her sight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_impairment "Visual impairment") and [her hearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deafness "Deafness") after a bout of illness when she was 19 months old. She then communicated primarily using [home signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_sign "Home sign") until the age of seven, when she met her first teacher and life-long companion [Anne Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Sullivan "Anne Sullivan"). Sullivan taught Keller language, including reading and writing. After an education at both specialist and mainstream schools, Keller attended [Radcliffe College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radcliffe_College "Radcliffe College") of [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") and became the first deafblind person in the United States to earn a college diploma.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Keller was also a prolific author, writing 14 books and hundreds of speeches and essays on topics ranging from animals to [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi").[[2]](#cite_note-2) Keller campaigned for those with [disabilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability "Disability") and for [women's suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage "Women's suffrage"), [labor rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_rights "Labor rights"), and [world peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_peace "World peace"). In 1909, she joined the [Socialist Party of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_of_America "Socialist Party of America") (SPA). She was a founding member of the [American Civil Liberties Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_Liberties_Union "American Civil Liberties Union") (ACLU).[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Keller's autobiography, *[The Story of My Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_of_My_Life_(biography) "The Story of My Life (biography)")* (1903), publicized her education and life with Sullivan. The playwright [William Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Gibson_(playwright) "William Gibson (playwright)") wrote a theatrical adaptation, *[The Miracle Worker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Miracle_Worker "The Miracle Worker")*, in 1959, which he adapted as [a film under the same title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Miracle_Worker_(1962_film) "The Miracle Worker (1962 film)") in 1962. **Martha Graham** (May 11, 1894 – April 1, 1991)[[1]](#cite_note-1) was an American modern dancer, teacher and choreographer responsible for creating the [Graham technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_technique "Graham technique").[[2]](#cite_note-TIME-2)

Graham danced and taught for over seventy years. She was the first dancer to perform at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), travel abroad as a cultural ambassador, and receive the highest civilian award of the US: the [Presidential Medal of Freedom with Distinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom"). In her lifetime she received honors including the [Key to the City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") of Paris and Japan's Imperial [Order of the Precious Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Precious_Crown "Order of the Precious Crown").

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Martha_Graham&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Graham was born in [Allegheny City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny, Pennsylvania"), later to become part of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Pennsylvania, in 1894. Her father, George Graham, was an "alienist", a practitioner of an early form of [psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatry "Psychiatry").[[3]](#cite_note-3) The Grahams were [Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterians "Presbyterians"). Her father was a third-generation American of Irish descent. Graham's mother, Jane Beers, was a second-generation American of Irish, Scots-Irish, and English ancestry, and who claimed to be a tenth-generation descendant[[4]](#cite_note-4) of [Myles Standish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myles_Standish "Myles Standish").[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) While her parents provided a comfortable environment in her youth, it was not one that encouraged dancing.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199812-7)

The Graham family moved to [Santa Maria, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria,_California "Santa Maria, California"), when Martha was fourteen years old.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199820-8) In 1911, she attended the first dance performance of her life, watching [Ruth St. Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_St._Denis "Ruth St. Denis") perform at the [Mason Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_Opera_House "Mason Opera House") in Los Angeles.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199821-9) In the mid-1910s, Martha Graham began her studies at the newly created [Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denishawn_School_of_Dancing_and_Related_Arts "Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts"), founded by Ruth St. Denis and [Ted Shawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Shawn "Ted Shawn"),[[10]](#cite_note-BryantPratt94-10) at which she would stay until 1923. In 1922, Graham performed one of Shawn's Egyptian dances with [Lillian Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Powell "Lillian Powell") in a short silent film by [Hugo Riesenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Riesenfeld "Hugo Riesenfeld") that attempted to synchronize a dance routine on film with a live orchestra and an onscreen conductor.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Martha_Graham&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Graham left the Denishawn establishment in 1923 in order to become a featured dancer in the [Greenwich Village Follies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village_Follies "Greenwich Village Follies") revue for two years.

In 1925, Graham was employed at the [Eastman School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastman_School_of_Music "Eastman School of Music") where [Rouben Mamoulian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouben_Mamoulian "Rouben Mamoulian") was head of the School of Drama. Among other performances, together Mamoulian and Graham produced a short [two-color film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_motion_picture_film "Color motion picture film") called *The Flute of Krishna,* featuring Eastman students. Mamoulian left Eastman shortly thereafter and Graham chose to leave also, even though she was asked to stay on.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In 1926, the [Martha Graham Center of Contemporary Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham_Center_of_Contemporary_Dance "Martha Graham Center of Contemporary Dance") was established, in a small studio on the [Upper East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_East_Side "Upper East Side") of New York City. On April 18 of the same year[[10]](#cite_note-BryantPratt94-10) Graham debuted her first independent concert, consisting of 18 short solos and trios that she had choreographed. This performance took place at the [48th Street Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_Street_Theatre "48th Street Theatre") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). She would later say of the concert: "Everything I did was influenced by [Denishawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denishawn "Denishawn")."[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMansfield_Soares199256-12) On November 28, 1926, Graham and others in her company gave a dance recital at the [Klaw Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaw_Theatre "Klaw Theatre") in New York City. Around the same time she entered an extended collaboration with Japanese-American [pictorialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictorialism "Pictorialism") photographer [Soichi Sunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soichi_Sunami "Soichi Sunami").[[13]](#cite_note-13) Graham was on the faculty of [Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhood_Playhouse_School_of_the_Theatre "Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre") when it opened in 1928.[[14]](#cite_note-peck-14)

One of Graham's students was heiress [Bethsabée de Rothschild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethsabée_de_Rothschild "Bethsabée de Rothschild") with whom she became close friends. When Rothschild moved to Israel and established the [Batsheva Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batsheva_Dance_Company "Batsheva Dance Company") in 1965, Graham became the company's first director.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

[Graham's technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_technique "Graham technique") pioneered a principle known as "contraction and release" in modern dance, which was derived from a stylized conception of breathing.[[16]](#cite_note-CraineMackrell2010-16)

In conjunction with the [1936 Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympic_Games "1936 Summer Olympic Games") in Berlin, the German government wanted to include dance in the Art Competitions that took place during the Olympics, an event that previously included architecture, sculpture, painting, music, and literature.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Although [Joseph Goebbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Goebbels "Joseph Goebbels"), Reich Minister of Propaganda, was not appreciative of the modern dance art form and changed Germany's dance from more avant-garde to traditional, he and [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") still agreed to invite Graham to represent the United States. However, the United States was not represented in the Art Competitions as Graham refused the invitation by stating:

> I would find it impossible to dance in Germany at the present time. So many artists whom I respect and admire have been persecuted, have been deprived of the right to work for ridiculous and unsatisfactory reasons, that I should consider it impossible to identify myself, by accepting the invitation, with the regime that has made such things possible. In addition, some of my concert group would not be welcomed in Germany.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanley2004136-18)

Goebbels himself wrote her a letter assuring her that her Jewish dancers would "receive complete immunity". Graham nevertheless rejected the invitation.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanley2004137-19)

Stimulated by the occurrences of the 1936 Olympic Games, and the propaganda that she heard through the radio from the [Axis powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers"), Graham created *[American Document](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Document "American Document")* in 1938. The dance expressed American ideals and democracy as Graham realized that it could empower men and inspire them to fight fascist and Nazi ideologies. American Document ended up as a patriotic statement focusing on rights and injustices of the time, representing the American people including its Native-American heritage and slavery. During the performance, excerpts from the [U.S. Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Independence_(U.S.) "Declaration of Independence (U.S.)"), Lincoln's [Gettysburg Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg_Address "Gettysburg Address"), and the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation") were read. These were passages that highlighted the American ideals and represented what made the American people American. For Graham, a dance needed to "reveal certain national characteristics because without these characteristics the dance would have no validity, no roots, no direct relation to life".[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In 1938, the [Roosevelt family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_family "Roosevelt family") invited Graham to dance at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), making her the first dancer to perform there.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In the same year, [Erick Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erick_Hawkins "Erick Hawkins") became the first man to dance with her company. He officially joined her troupe the following year, dancing male lead in a number of Graham's works. They were married in July 1948 after the New York premiere of *Night Journey*.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFranko2012139-22) He left her troupe in 1951 and they divorced in 1954.

On April 1, 1958, the [Martha Graham Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham_Dance_Company "Martha Graham Dance Company") premiered the ballet *[Clytemnestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clytemnestra_(dance) "Clytemnestra (dance)")*, which would become a success.[[23]](#cite_note-23) With a score by Egyptian-born composer [Halim El-Dabh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halim_El-Dabh "Halim El-Dabh"), this ballet was a large scale work and the only full-length work in Graham's career. Graham choreographed and danced the title role, spending almost the entire duration of the performance on the stage.[[24]](#cite_note-lamothe-24) The ballet tells the story of Queen [Clytemnestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clytemnestra "Clytemnestra"), who is married to King [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon").

# Anderson (crater)

Anderson

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [LRO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Reconnaissance_Orbiter "Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter") image | |
| [Coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenographic_coordinates "Selenographic coordinates") | [15°48′N 171°06′E﻿ / ﻿15.8°N 171.1°E﻿ / 15.8; 171.1](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Anderson_(crater)&params=15.8_N_171.1_E_globe:moon_type:landmark) |
| [Diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter "Diameter") | 105.33 km (65.45 mi)[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1) |
| [Depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crater_depth "Crater depth") | *Unknown* |

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Anderson_crater_LROC.jpg/330px-Anderson_crater_LROC.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

**Anderson** is a [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_crater "Lunar crater") [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") that is located on the [far side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_side_(Moon) "Far side (Moon)") of the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon").[[2]](#cite_note-Moore_2000-2) It lies within the [Freundlich-Sharonov Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freundlich-Sharonov_Basin "Freundlich-Sharonov Basin"), and is located to the northwest of the crater [Sharonov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharonov_(lunar_crater) "Sharonov (lunar crater)").[[3]](#cite_note-Byrne_2008-3) The satellite crater Sharanov X is attached to the southeast rim of Anderson. To the northeast is the peculiar formation [Buys-Ballot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buys-Ballot_(crater) "Buys-Ballot (crater)"), and to the east-southeast lies the larger crater [Spencer Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Jones_(crater) "Spencer Jones (crater)").

The outer rim of Anderson is heavily worn and eroded. Small craters overlie the southeastern and southwestern rims. The interior is relatively flat, with multiple tiny craters covering parts of the floor. The most prominent of these is Anderson L, located near the southeastern rim.[[4]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-4): 68 The infrared spectrum of pure crystalline [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase "Plagioclase") has been identified on the northeast and southeast rim, along with ejecta to the northeast.[[5]](#cite_note-Donaldson_Hanna_et_al_2014-5)

This crater is named after American astronomer [John A. Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_August_Anderson "John August Anderson") (1876–1959).[[6]](#cite_note-Menzel_et_al_1971-6) Its designation was formally adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 1970.[[1]](#cite_note-GPN-1)

## Satellite craters

By convention these features are identified on lunar maps by placing the letter on the side of the crater midpoint that is closest to Anderson.[[7]](#cite_note-Grego_2015-7)

| Anderson[[4]](#cite_note-Bussey_Spudis_2004-4): 291 | Latitude | Longitude | Diameter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E | 16.9° N | 173.4° E | 28 km |
| F | 16.3° N | 173.6° E | 49 km |
| L | 14.6° N | 170.9° E | 14 km |

Anderson E and F have [fractured floors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_moon_with_fractured_floors "List of craters on the moon with fractured floors").[[8]](#cite_note-Wilhelms_et_al_1987-8) Both date to the [Nectarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nectarian "Nectarian") period of the [lunar geologic timescale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_geologic_timescale "Lunar geologic timescale").[[9]](#cite_note-Gustafson_2012-9)
